Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q2 2024 FTAI Aviation Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you would need to press star one one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would like now to turn the conference over to Alan Andreini, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Alan Andreini
Head of Investor Relations, FTAI Aviation
Thank you, Michelle. I would like to welcome you all to the FTAI Aviation Q2 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me here today are Joe Adams, our Chief Executive Officer, Angela Nam, our Chief Financial Officer, and David Moreno, our Chief Operating Officer. We have posted an investor presentation in our press release on our website, which we encourage you to download if you have not already done so. Also, please note that this call is open to the public in listen-only mode and is being webcast.
In addition, we will be discussing some non-GAAP financial measures during the call today, including EBITDA. The reconciliation of those measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures can be found in the earnings supplement. Before I turn the call over to Joe, I would like to point out that certain statements made today will be forward-looking statements, including regarding future earnings.
These statements, by their nature, are uncertain and may differ materially from actual results. We encourage you to review the disclaimers in our press release and investor presentation regarding non-GAAP financial measures and forward-looking statements, and to review the risk factors contained in our quarterly report filed with the SEC. Now I would like to turn the call over to Joe.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thank you, Alan. To start today, I'm pleased to announce our 37th dividend as a public company and our 52nd consecutive dividend since inception. The dividend of $0.30 per share will be paid on 20 August, based on a shareholder record date of 12 August. Now let's turn to the numbers. The key metric for us is adjusted EBITDA. We continued the year strongly with adjusted EBITDA of $213.9 million in Q2 2024, which is up 30% compared to $164.1 million in Q1 of this year, and up 40% compared to $153.1 million in Q2 of 2023.
During Q2, the $213.9 million EBITDA number was comprised of $125 million from our Leasing segment, $91.2 million from our Aerospace Products segment, and -$2.3 million from corporate and other. Turning now to Leasing. Leasing had a great quarter, posting approximately $125 million of EBITDA. The pure Leasing component of the $125 million came in at $112 million for Q2 versus $98 million in Q1 of 2024. Additionally, we sold $59 million book value of assets for a gain of $13.5 million.
With exceptionally strong demand for assets and the continuation of a robust Northern Hemisphere summer travel season, we now expect to generate $500 million in EBITDA in 2024, which includes $50 million in gains on asset sales versus our prior estimate of $475 million. Aerospace products had yet another excellent quarter with $91.2 million of EBITDA at an overall EBITDA margin of 37%. We're seeing tremendous growth in the aerospace products business in general and feel good about raising our estimates for 2024 EBITDA in aerospace products from our prior estimate of $250 million up to $325 to 350 million.
We also are experiencing expansion in aerospace products margins as demand for refurbished modules and engines remains very high, while increasing efficiencies at our two CFM56 maintenance facilities in Montreal and Miami is controlling or in some cases lowering our costs. Overall, looking ahead, we now expect annual aviation EBITDA for 2024 to be between $825 million and $850 million, not counting corporate and other versus our original estimate of $675 to 725 million. Finally, about two years ago, we first outlined our corporate financial goal of generating in 2026 $1 billion of EBITDA, comprised of $500 million from leasing and $500 million from aerospace products. Now that we're halfway through this time period and ahead of plan, we're resetting the target.
Our new goal is $1.25 billion of EBITDA in 2026, comprised of $550 million of leasing EBITDA and $700 million of aerospace products EBITDA. With that, I'll turn the call back to Alan.
Alan Andreini
Head of Investor Relations, FTAI Aviation
Thank you, Joe. Michelle, you may now open the call to Q&A.
Hello?
Operator
The first question comes from Jason Holcomb with Morgan Stanley. Your line is now open.
Jason Holcomb
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Morgan Stanley
Good morning, Joe, Angela, and David.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Morning.
Angela Nam
CFO, FTAI Aviation
Morning.
Jason Holcomb
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Morgan Stanley
Well, within Aerospace Products, you've historically mentioned that you target EBITDA margin of around 35%. The last couple of quarters, we've seen you surpass that target. It would be great if you could talk about where you see margins going from here as you continue to grow and develop the business. Also it'd be great if you could speak to how that margin path may differ between both the CFM56 and the V2500 engines. Thank you.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Great. Thanks for the question. Yes, we are, as I mentioned in the remarks, we are seeing margins trending up, and it's fairly basic. It's our revenues are going up and our expenses are either flat or down. The revenue side is really demand-based, where, as you can realize it, equipment is in short supply, turn times at maintenance shops are getting longer. That means it puts a premium on having a pre-built engine or module available. So we can actually, you know, get higher, slightly higher prices and still generate significant savings for the customers. At the same time, you know, by controlling costs through our own facilities, we do that with controlling the labor cost and that we have more specialization in the facilities.
We're basically running, you know, one engine, and we're teaching people to do it in a high volume way, you know, manner. It's a learning curve process where you get better and better at it as you do it more and more frequently. That's part of it. We're also getting smarter about used serviceable material, forecasting the demand, where is it gonna be needed? When are we gonna need it, getting our repairs done in advance. We're using, you know, we're smarter and more efficient about using used material. It's really on, you know, on both sides of the equation, revenues up, expenses down, that we see growing margins. We will also see increased savings when we close on Lockheed Martin.
We do see the margins trending towards 40%, and we think that will continue to grow as we get better and more experienced with that facility as well, and we generate more volume. You know, pretty positive outlook for today and also for the near future, for the coming years. I would say on your other question on Pratt versus CFM, we have said that the Pratt & Whitney V2500 deal will not be dilutive to margins, and I would continue to say that. We're seeing very good demand for those engines, extremely high. We're also, you know, seeing good turnaround times on getting engines through the shop.
We continue to expect that will be the same or as good as or better than the CFM side.
Jason Holcomb
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Morgan Stanley
All right. Thank you for that, Joe. I'll leave it at one.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Sheila Kahyaoglu with Jefferies. Your line is open.
Kyle Wenclawiak
Equity Research Senior Associate, Jefferies
Hi, team. This is Kyle Wenclawiak on for Sheila.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Hello.
Kyle Wenclawiak
Equity Research Senior Associate, Jefferies
Hey, guys. Very nice quarter here and H1 really in Aero Products. It's not just the EBITDA growth, but the margins, like you just said, kind of trending towards 40% is now kind of the watermark. Maybe just drilling in on your comments, Joe, about the Lockheed facility. How are you thinking about the margin opportunity within that facility as that deal is gonna close in H2 and kind of what it means for the productivity, the throughput, and the piece part opportunity there for the modules?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah. Good question. I think that we've indicated we expect about $30 million of savings per annum once we close on initially just on the CFM56 overhaul operations. That should add, you know, 3 to 4 percentage points to the margins just from that closing. I think the efficiency, we haven't really baked that in yet, but we did see quite an improvement when we took control of the Miami facility. We've seen a pretty significant increase in throughput per person. So we expect a similar trend in that facility, although we don't yet, you know, have our hands on it. It's something we think, you know, we'll be able to accomplish, and we don't see any reason because we've done it before.
Lastly, incremental to that is the piece part repair business, which we've talked about for quite some time, and there's a lot of capability in the Lockheed Martin facility that was not really fully developed. We're going to accelerate the development of the piece part repair business. We're gonna do more repairs for our own engines, repairs for third parties, and then we'll develop new repairs. That I've indicated we expect to generate probably an incremental $10 to 15 million of EBITDA from that over, but not really starting until probably 2025, and then potentially growing from there. We'll update you on that.
We see, you know, this every time we look at the engine and we look at, you know, something new, we find, you know, millions of dollars lying on the floor. There's so many opportunities that we can pursue that are big dollars. So we're very optimistic that we're gonna. We'll keep. This is continuous improvement, is what we've always said over the last, you know, five, six years, and we're nowhere near the end of our list of opportunities.
Kyle Wenclawiak
Equity Research Senior Associate, Jefferies
Great. Super helpful. I'll leave it at one. Thanks, guys.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Josh Sullivan with The Benchmark Company. Your line is open.
Josh Sullivan
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Hey, good morning. Congratulations on the quarter here. What is the relative turnaround time for an airline or a lessor using the module factory versus the open market at this point?
David Moreno
COO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah, I can take that. This is David. The typical industry turn time, what we're seeing is anything from 120 days to 180 days. Our turn time on modules is about 30 to 60 days to actually build a module, right? Then to actually execute said module, depends on the module, is anywhere from five to 25 days. For a customer's perspective, they're doing the module swap in five to 25 days versus 120 to 180 days. We're seeing industry turn times that are long and getting longer. I think we're in a much better position, predominantly for four reasons, right? Number one is we have capacity up in Montreal and in Miami.
We have the capacity and the workforce. Number two is we have access to used serviceable material via our AAR program. Number three is what Joe mentioned, is we have access to repairs at Lockheed, where we can repair parts. Number four, we have the flexibility since it's our fleet of mixing and matching modules as well as planning. As we see turn times go down industry-wide, I think it is accelerating more and more demand for modules because one of the key attributes of modules is it's a faster product than a traditional MRO.
Josh Sullivan
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Got it. Just as a follow-up on the piece part repair business expansion, is that an organic effort or do you see opportunities to bolt on inorganically at Montreal?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Both. I think that our base case is organic, but, you know, we have a lot of conversations. You know, we've been engaging with different parties in that business for the last two years, looking at different alternatives. There might be some combination of the two, which is organic plus, you know, working with another player in the industry. We are always open-minded and flexible, and, you know, however, whatever, you know, the math and the operations, you know, would support, we'll take a look at it. There's not enough capacity in the piece part repair business globally.
We realized that last year, I think we spent $50 million with third parties where we're a pretty big buyer of repair services, and no one had ever called on us and marketed a product to us. It's amazing. The industry is all order takers. There's a lot of, you know, things that we think, you know, we can do to grow and increase that business, you know, we're just at the very beginning of that.
Josh Sullivan
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Great. Thank you for the time.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yep.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Hillary Cacanando with Deutsche Bank. Your line is open.
Hillary Cacanando
Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank
Thank you. Good morning. You had previously mentioned that savings this year from internalization would be about $30 million. Given that you're raising guidance, does that number change? You know, do you now expect more savings from internalization for 2024? You know, how should we think about that number for 2025 and beyond?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yes, it will go up as we've increased our expectations for this year and for the out year 2026. We had indicated at the time of the internalization we would save $30 million annually, which we think, you know, we'll do at least that this year, and that number will grow to $40 million or $50 million in the next couple of years, and then potentially higher than that. I mean, we're very confident that the numbers that we'll save are better than what we had thought, what we expected, you know, a couple of months ago.
Hillary Cacanando
Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank
Okay. For modeling purposes, we could probably assume, like, $30 million this year and then maybe, like, $40 to 50 million next year, and then maybe even higher in 2026.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah.
Hillary Cacanando
Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank
Kind of upward trending in terms of savings.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yes.
Hillary Cacanando
Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank
Okay, perfect. In slide number eight in the leasing segment, it says that you performed 10 engine exchanges for aircraft leases year to date. I think this is the first time you've discussed engine exchanges with your lessees. Could you just go over exactly what that is and if those 10 engine exchanges are included in the 82 modules sold number? You know, are these, like, engine exchanges with your lessees one-offs or do you have contracts with them to do more?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah. I'll let David walk through that.
David Moreno
COO, FTAI Aviation
Hey, Hillary. The answer is in addition to the 82. On our entire aircraft portfolio, we manage the shop visits via exchanges. We're manufacturing engines ahead of removals and providing exchanges instead of lessees doing shop visits, which is typically how these contracts are written. It's a value add. The reason why we like it is because we're able to charge OEM rates per the contract for every hour and cycle flown. We're able to manufacture those engines for a lot less. That margin is going to show up through the maintenance revenue on our financial statements. The reason why airlines like it is because they're able to avoid the major shop visits. They have zero turn time.
Typically, they'd have to lease an engine during that interim period, which can be very expensive, as well as they are responsible for the most part on all negative surprises. If the shop visit overruns, typically the airline would be in charge of that over and above. They really like that service. It's a value-add as part of our aircraft leasing business.
Hillary Cacanando
Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank
Okay. Well, thank you so much, David. Thank you. Thank you, Joe.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah. It goes to the, you know, when we talk about our business model is basically, we are in the engine maintenance business. Most lessors are in the maintenance avoidance business, and they force it onto the airline, and we're the opposite. We want to do the maintenance, and we want the airlines to get out of the maintenance business because we're better at it. It's really. We're providing an outsourced opportunity for airlines to not have to manage shop visits, which for the most part, most airlines are not particularly good at.
Hillary Cacanando
Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank
I'm sure when you're talking to potential lessees, this is something that you pitch as well, right? Like, if we could do exchanges as well. That's probably a selling point, I'm assuming.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yes. We're saving them time and money, and eliminating a major, you know, possible negative surprise in a lease.
Hillary Cacanando
Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank
Okay. Thank you very much.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Giuliano Bologna with Compass Point. Your line is open.
Giuliano Bologna
Managing Director, Compass Point
Good morning, y'all. Congratulations on another incredible quarter, especially on the product side of the business. As a first question, I'd be curious, looking at the leasing side of the business, you know, you outperformed, you know, pretty strongly, especially on, even on core leasing. I'm curious, you know, what drove the leasing outperformance and if, you know, that's a trend that we should expect to continue going forward.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah. The two big drivers are rent and hours, flying. Both of those are up. It's very, you know, the rent market, as you're probably obviously aware, you know, with the demand for equipment, and particularly older equipment that we own, is quite high. Airlines around the world are extending leases and not giving those back, given that they can't get, they can't fly a lot of GTF-powered engine aircraft, and they can't get deliveries from Boeing on time. So the demand for older equipment and engines related to those is very high. And then typically Q2 and really Q3 are, you know, very high utilization quarters for airlines, because the demand is there for flying. So we see it in the maintenance revenues as well.
It's both rent and maintenance reserves are up.
Giuliano Bologna
Managing Director, Compass Point
That's very helpful. You know, thinking about the shortage of engines globally and, you know, a lot of the supply chain issues that are out there. You know, there are a few industry leaders have suggested that the industry will, you know, take or normalize, you know, or won't normalize until somewhere between late 2026 and 2030. I'm curious, you know, how you think about what that means for the opportunity for FTAI and also, you know, what normalization would mean or look like, you know, on the other side of that. I realize it's pretty far out, so there's a pretty good runway here.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah. We have always, you know, thought to run our business assuming normalization. This is just you know an unexpected gift that we got. We think we have a great business even in an environment where, you know, everything is smooth, running, and functionally well. Having said that, you know, it is difficult to project, but I also would point out that it's not gonna be a cliff. You're not gonna wake up in 2027, and all of a sudden everything is good. It'll be a gradual, you know, return to normalization over some, you know, extended period of time because as you see, fixing supply chains, hiring people back is a very lengthy process, and it only takes one part of that supply chain to negatively affect the entire supply chain.
I think it'll be, you know, probably what everybody, you know, generally the extremes are not right. It's somewhere in the middle. Somebody says 2030, somebody says 2026, it's probably in the middle, but it's a gradual, you know, return to normal, not all of a sudden a bright line event.
Giuliano Bologna
Managing Director, Compass Point
That's very helpful. Then one last one. Thinking about the product segment and kind of the demand for CFM56s and LEAP-1As. I'm curious what the pipeline or the order backlog looks like, you know, in Q3 and Q4 relative to Q2. You know, how we should think about what that pipeline is already, you know, indicating or telling us.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
We have some long-term contracts, like if you talk about WestJet and LATAM or Avianca, where we have, you know, six to eight-year deals locked in. We have very good visibility on that type of business. The other, more transactional, you know, is probably we have three to six-month visibility. We're getting people to give us forecasts of when they're going to need equipment earlier so that we can, as David said, we can order material, we can plan better, we can have the modules ready.
I would say our visibility is getting longer than it was, you know, even a year ago. We're encouraging airlines to really be, you know, Once they've tasted, you know, and experienced the product and they like it, they say, "Well, okay, now give us your, you know, give us all your business and give us your program and give us your profile when you're gonna need it." I think we're gonna continue to push for more programs, more visibility, and longer, you know, time to get ready, and everybody benefits from that.
Giuliano Bologna
Managing Director, Compass Point
That is, very helpful. I appreciate it. Yeah, congrats on the quarter, and I will jump back into queue.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Ken Herbert with RBC. Your line is open.
Ken Herbert
Managing Director, RBC
Yeah. Hey, Joe. Good morning.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Good morning.
Ken Herbert
Managing Director, RBC
Hey, I just wanted to ask you know, you did 82 modular swaps this quarter. What percentage of the global sort of CFM56 operator universe are you currently working with? And how quickly is that expanding, and what's sort of the timeframe as you think about an airline today with everything going on, you know, that may not have been a customer that comes to you and ultimately becomes a customer? Sort of how is that sales cycle compressing?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Lots of aspects to that question. We indicated that we have now 50 customers in, you know, our module factory. If you think back in 2022 when we sort of rolled out our math for getting to $1 billion, we were forecasting 50 by 2026. We're now at 50 in 2024. Things are moving quickly. Part of, you know, what happens in a crisis is when people, you know, need something, then they're more receptive to changing their business model. We see that the current environment is accelerating people's transitioning to outsourcing maintenance, engine maintenance, which is what we're offering the customer. Those 50 represent what we'll say 300 total potential.
Maybe we're, you know, 1/6 of the operator base, and we're not getting. With a couple of exceptions, we're not getting 100% of people's business yet. But we're aspiring to because we don't see any reason why we shouldn't once people realize they can, you know, save, they save money, they save time, and they eliminate negative surprises. It's like, how hard, you know, what else do you need me to tell you? I think it's still growing. It's a huge market. The total universe, if you think about, you know, 3,000 shop visits a year, and you can argue whether it's 4,000 or 2,500 or something, but roughly 3,000, that's 9,000 modules moving through a maintenance facility somewhere in the world per year.
We're talking about doing, you know, 400, 500. It's still less than 10%. It's half of 10%. We're not anywhere near, you know, where we think the penetration could get to. We have our own maintenance capacity. We can do 300 shop visits in Montreal a year, which is 900 modules, and 150 in Miami, which is 450 modules. We have 1,350, you know, module rebuild capacity that we own now. If you think about 400 or 500 is what we're, you know, shooting for, that's 5% market penetration. We can handle 15% today based on what we own. You know, we're in a pretty good position to keep growing that.
We haven't had anybody that used the product that didn't wanna do it again. That, to me, is one of the main litmus tests is that, you know, do people like it, and did they have a good experience? That's what we're trying to foster so that the word of mouth spreads. People put, you know, testimonials up on their Instagram accounts, and they talk about how great this is. We have photos of people in maintenance facilities that can say, "I just did a LPT swap in two weeks, and, you know, that engine would have been in the shop for, you know, six months if I hadn't done that." Those are the kind of things we're, you know, the viral marketing that we're using to accelerate even more. I might have missed.
There are a lot of elements to your question, but I don't know if I got all of them, but.
Ken Herbert
Managing Director, RBC
No, that's great. If I could just one follow-up. I mean, obviously, you know, you're benefiting from the supply chain disruptions, turnaround times, and lead times on material, but you obviously also buy a lot of material to fulfill demand while we're waiting for, you know, PMA parts and other stuff. Are you seeing an extension in the material you're looking to buy, you know, the new OEM material or even on the USM side? Has that been maybe a headwind to some of the throughput?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
It's like, I mean, there's two parts. There's the CFM part and the Pratt part. You talk about the CFM
David Moreno
COO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
I'll talk about Pratt.
David Moreno
COO, FTAI Aviation
Sure. On the CFM side, yes, we are seeing a delay for, let's say, repairing parts. I think we're well-positioned because we have the inventory ahead of time, right? We are tearing down, you know, 40 to 50 engines per year with AAR. We're able to recall those parts and use them ahead of time. Really, it's, you know, having the USM available, and then number two is planning, right? Before a module comes into the shop, we understand, and we have a kitting process ahead of time. We produce the kit on what exactly is needed in that module. We're able to be one step, you know, ahead in that process, right?
Typically, what would happen is if you're engaging in third-party work, an engine would show up, and you'd have a very limited amount of time to react and order parts, right? That's all happening ahead of time. We feel like we're well-positioned, and that's why our turn times have not been impacted.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
On the V2500, I mean, we just spent time with Pratt last week, and we're talking about, you know, material availability and turn times, and they're very confident. I mean, earlier this year they had some sort of delays in producing some of the V2500 parts and material, but they're on top of it now. They're very confident, and we are, I would say, a high priority customer. With an order of 100 shop visits, we get, you know, they're gonna put us, you know, at the top of the list. They're very confident that what they've indicated us, the 90-day turn times, that they're gonna deliver on that.
It's also, you know, it's helpful from our point of view that we're very flexible, and they can put those engines into whatever shop in their network they want to. That they indicated was very helpful because they can use, you know, our orders to fill in shops that don't have enough business yet.
Alan Andreini
Head of Investor Relations, FTAI Aviation
Great. Thank you very much.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Brandon Oglinski with Barclays. Your line is open.
Brandon Oglenski
Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Barclays
Hey, good morning, everyone, and thanks for taking my question. Joe, I appreciate the updated guidance for this year and you know, longer-term outlook on the business. I guess, though, with how tight the market is, I mean, I know you're generating better margins now, but when we think of acquisition costs, especially for new engines, does this get more challenging looking ahead, or is it the swap aspect that makes this so viable?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah, that's a great question. We've been pretty good at sourcing engines, and I think the main reason is we tend to excel when an engine is in need of a shop visit in the immediate or near future. If you think about most buyers when, you know, a portfolio or an aircraft comes up and they do their model, and they have to do a shop visit in the next, you know, 18, 6 to 24 months, it's a huge negative to them. We're one of the few buyers that actually, when we see a shop visit in the near future, we're like, "This is great.
We love this, because we know we're gonna A, we can do the shop visit generally for less than other people can, and B, we can also, you know, optimize by doing module swaps. We can sometimes do hospital shop repairs. We can generate more, you know, we can burn off some of the green time that other people, you know, can't value. We have so many ways to make that into a better deal than virtually anybody else that we win a disproportionate amount of that business. There's a lot of engines out there that during COVID people didn't do any maintenance on. We're seeing a lot of a very good pipeline of acquisition opportunities. That is one of our core strengths, is sourcing, you know, run-out engines.
That's the first part of, you know, our business model, which is to buy run-out engines, then we fix them up, and then we lease them, sell them, or exchange them. We love the exchange option, too, because then you're getting another engine back that's run out, generally at a very good price because you're solving somebody's problem, and you also then get to do it all over again. It's a virtuous circle for us in sourcing.
Brandon Oglenski
Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Barclays
Okay. I appreciate that, Joe. I guess as you transition more earnings and the business mix to aviation products, how should investors think about free cash flow in the business? Maybe, you know, longer term, where do you want to see leverage on the balance sheet too? Thank you, Joe.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah. The second question, we've just did an $800 million high-yield deal, and we indicated that our goal is to be strong BB by all agencies and have debt to total EBITDA in the 3x to 3.5x range. This quarter, we're at 3.4x. The bonds have traded up. I think we're trading, you know, pretty much like a BB, strong BB at the moment. That's something we think is, you know, achievable this year and in the near future. We're gonna maintain that leverage and that rating.
In terms of free cash flow, what we do is we take the EBITDA, subtract corporate and interest, and then we use a number for maintenance CapEx, what we need to invest each year to maintain the engines so that they can fly, you know, forever ad infinitum. That number tends to be between $60 million and $80 million a year of maintenance CapEx. When you run the math, we'll generate hundreds of millions of free cash flow in the near future.
That's been our goal since, you know, as you remember back from 2022 when we set those targets, is not to be in a perpetual cycle of always buying more equipment, but just turning it faster and generating a lot of cash.
Brandon Oglenski
Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Barclays
Thanks for that. Appreciate it.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Stephen Trent with Citi. Your line is now open.
Stephen Trent
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Citi
Good morning, everybody, and thanks very much for taking my question. You know, I recall you commented about your global footprint and opportunities you saw to expand, for example. I believe you previously called out Southeast Asia geographically. I was wondering since that time, you know, what sort of elements you've seen in the market that might be reinforcing your view on that being an attractive footprint. Thank you.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
David Moreno
COO, FTAI Aviation
Hi, Stephen, I can take that question. This is David. Yes, Southeast Asia is a very important region for us. It has a high concentration of 737 NGs and A320s. Typically that fleet has been newer, and now with time it's maturing and the engines are due shop visits. It's an area that we're keenly focused on. Recently, we started working with an airline by doing all module swaps at their hangar facility. They have a hangar, where they do airframe work and light engine work as well. We started doing module swaps on LPTs. We have a large program with that airline. And we've also recently started offering that as a third-party business. Now we have airlines coming in with aircraft that have engines that need module swaps.
We are performing those module swaps for that airline, and the aircraft is going back in the air in 15 to 20 days. It's operating like a pit stop. We've started with a few third-party customers, and we're very excited to grow that, you know, presence in Southeast Asia.
Stephen Trent
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Citi
I appreciate that, David. Very helpful. Just as a follow-up, you know, on the M&A side, you guys seem to be really putting together a potent story on MRO, and I know you've done your own acquisitions like QuickTurn and what have you. Long term, would you ever consider, you know, a larger competitor acquiring you?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Well, I mean, it's up to the shareholders. We're always, you know, we're very shareholder oriented, so we all own a lot of stock. You know, if the right offer came in and somebody was interested, we would certainly entertain it. It's also a board-level call, not just an individual, so.
Stephen Trent
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Citi
Fair enough, and I appreciate that, Joe. Thank you for the time.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Brian McKenna with Citizens JMP. Your line is open.
Brian McKenna
Director of Equity Research, Citizens JMP
All right, great. Thanks. Good morning, everyone. Most questions have been asked, but it would be great just to get an update on capital management. I'm assuming returns on new investments today are quite high, so I suspect your top priority for capital is investing back into the business for longer term growth. Can you just walk through your capital priorities today as it relates to new investments, further deleveraging, strategic M&A, and then dividends and buybacks?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yes. First priority is to achieve and maintain the strong BB rating, which I mentioned, and maintain debt at, you know, 3x to 3.5x debt to total EBITDA, so that we're on course. We, you know, are in that zone in Q2, and we expect by the end of the year to be solidly in that. That's priority number one. Priority number two, as you mentioned, is investments. We do have a good pipeline of acquisitions. We also are turning that by selling modules and engines quicker. Our goal is not to, you know, have a huge increase in net assets owned this year.
Having said that, at the beginning of the year, we did indicate with the V2500 program, we expected to increase our engine count from roughly 60 V2500s at the beginning of this year to about 150 to 200 by the end of this year. We're well on our way. We're at 130 now, and so we expect to achieve that. That, you know, if you think of an average engine being $5 million or so, adding 100 engines adds about $500 million capital. That's been a focus this year, is to have the V2500. Once we achieve, you know, having 400 to 500 CFM56 engines and 150 to 200 V2500s, we don't need to grow that number significantly.
After that, it then becomes a question for shareholder returns, and dividends and stock buybacks would be the third priority.
Brian McKenna
Director of Equity Research, Citizens JMP
Okay, great. Helpful. Just one more follow-up for you, Joe. You know, just given how much the business has grown over the past couple of years, you know, how are you splitting your time between managing the two segments? You know, somewhat related, is there an opportunity to lean in on hiring here, just given the broader macro environment to further accelerate growth in some of the emerging opportunities within aerospace products?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Well, I spend 100% of my time on FTAI, whatever is needed, so I don't think of it as like splitting. You know, I've said to people, my dream is that one day people will not do a sum of the parts calculation and think of this as we do as an integrated product. We go to the airlines and we say, "Look, we can provide you your engine maintenance without you having to do it. You outsource it to us, and we'll always have an engine for you, and we'll save you time and money and provide you a lot of flexibility." That's our pitch. So what we do is we go buy runout engines, we rebuild them, and then we can offer either a lease, a sale, or an exchange to an airline.
The leasing is just one spoke, you know, one arm of what we offer. It's an important one because having that ability gives the airline the flexibility to say, "Well, you know what? I only want, you know, three years, I think is what I'm gonna need." Somebody else says, "I want six years." You have the ability to customize and say, whatever you want, we'll deliver, you know, that for you. That integrated product is extremely, you know, powerful. We don't think of it as two different businesses. We report it that way, but someday we'll, you know, hopefully people will stop doing some of the parts, and they'll say, "This is just a, you know, this is a great product.
This is an outsourced engine maintenance business for aftermarket for the most popular engines in the world.
Brian McKenna
Director of Equity Research, Citizens JMP
Yeah, got it. Makes sense. I'll leave it there, and congrats on another great quarter.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Myles Walton with Wolfe Research. Your line is open.
Myles Walton
Managing Director, Wolfe Research
Thanks. Good morning. Hey, Joe, I was wondering if you could maybe decompose the $700 million of EBITDA in 2026. The $500 million previously, I think, had $50 million of PMA, third-party parts, and couple hundred of million of better drop through in the module business. Is the PMA contribution to that $700 million about the same, and the remainder's better business elsewhere, plus the V2500?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yes. They are similar. PMA, USM, each about 50, and then we've added probably between 100 and 150 for the V2500 program. The rest is just higher margins and more volume on CFM modules.
Myles Walton
Managing Director, Wolfe Research
Does that higher margin volume on CFM require that PMA? 'Cause that was sort of the selling point to get to that higher margin. Or is the market now so robust that you don't need the PMA for that drop through?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
You know, we're gonna get it. You know, the PMA will come, and that will increase the margins. I think we're gonna increase margins even without PMA, but definitely we're planning on PMA increasing margins.
Myles Walton
Managing Director, Wolfe Research
Okay. There's been a lot of news about airlines, and clearly yields are working against them, and they're running more into cost questions about containment. Are you finding that this business that you have has more durability in a market where airlines are cost cutting? Where are your weak points? Where are your strengths if we go into that cash conservation mode that sometimes cyclically happens with airlines?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yes. It does help us and, you know, we're providing, as I said, cost savings. When everybody's told to look at every line item in the, you know, P&L, one of the line items that always pops up is engine maintenance as a big one, and one that they seem to never be able to get it to go down. We can provide, you know, a flattening out of that and savings. When people do have a, you know, intense focus on cost savings, then outsourcing of these types of activities goes up, the demand for that goes up. We're happy, you know, in any environment, but particularly when people are, you know, focusing on. That's what we're providing is expense management reduction.
Myles Walton
Managing Director, Wolfe Research
Yeah. Okay. All right. Great. I'll leave it there. Thank you.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for the next question. The next question comes from Sherif Elmaghrabi with BTIG. Your line is open.
Sherif Elmaghrabi
VP of Equity Research, BTIG
Hey, good morning. I wanna start with an update on PMA. How is industry acceptance going for your first part? Can you talk through what the second PMA part does within the engine and timing for approval there, please?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yeah, the timing we've said is shortly. You know, obviously we're closer today than we were last quarter. We don't forecast specific timing, but very good progress made on all fronts on that, so we're very confident. The first part we have installed in 15 engines, it's been flying with another airline and no issues. It's a high quality product as always with Chromalloy, and we think the industry acceptance is going to grow. There is a school of thought for many airlines that if they're gonna put PMA, they want more than one part, so there are airlines that will wait till there's more parts approved.
Once those are, you know, available, then we expect industry take-up to be quite robust. There's also, you know, an additional element today in supply chain availability in that it's not just cost savings for PMA, it's availability, which is also important that you have another alternative if you can't get in a timely manner the OEM parts.
Sherif Elmaghrabi
VP of Equity Research, BTIG
That's good color. On the corporate side, both of the well intervention vessels are now on charter, and it looks like the rate that they're earning has melted up nicely. How are you progressing on the sale of these vessels, and are there any recent transactions you can point to to give us a sense of how they're valued?
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Yes. You're right, the market is improving nicely. We have a handshake deal on both vessels today, which we expect to close by the end of the year, subject to a couple of conditions that we think will be met. The market has strengthened and we expect for the next few years it's gonna be a strong market. The vessels are both on charter doing well, generating EBITDA and the values have gone up. We originally said we thought we would get approximately $150 million, and we're in that zip code, so we're very happy with you know that the end of that chapter is close.
Sherif Elmaghrabi
VP of Equity Research, BTIG
Thanks for taking my questions, Joe.
Joe Adams
CEO, FTAI Aviation
Thanks.
Operator
I show no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn the call back over to Alan Andreini for closing remarks.
Alan Andreini
Head of Investor Relations, FTAI Aviation
Thank you all for participating in today's conference call. We look forward to updating you after Q3.
Operator
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
Operator
Good day and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q1 2022 Fortress Transportation and Infrastructure Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star one on your telephone. If you require any further assistance, please press star zero. I would now like to hand the conference over to our speaker today, Mr. Alan Andreini. Please go ahead.
Alan Andreini
Managing Director, Fortress Investment Group
Thank you, Tanya. I would like to welcome you to the Fortress Transportation and Infrastructure Q1 2022 Earnings Call. Joining me here today are Joe Adams, our Chief Executive Officer, Ken Nicholson, our newly appointed CEO of FTAI Infrastructure, Scott Christopher, the Chief Financial Officer of FTAI, who will become the CFO of FTAI Infrastructure, and Angela Nam, the Chief Accounting Officer of FTAI, who will become the CFO of FTAI Aviation, which will be the new name of FTAI. We have posted an investor presentation in our press release on our website, which we encourage you to download if you have not already done so. Also, please note that this call is open to the public in listen-only mode and is being webcast. In addition, we will be discussing some non-GAAP financial measures during the call today, including FAD.
The reconciliations of those measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures can be found in the earnings supplement. Before I turn the call over to Joe and Ken, I would like to point out that certain statements made today will be forward-looking statements, including regarding future earnings. These statements, by their nature, are uncertain and may differ materially from actual results. We encourage you to review the disclaimers in our press release and investor presentation regarding non-GAAP financial measures and forward-looking statements, and to review the risk factors contained in our quarterly report filed with the SEC. Now I would like to turn the call over to Joe.
Joe Adams
CEO, Fortress Transportation and Infrastructure
Thank you, Alan. To start the call, I'm pleased to announce our 28th dividend as a public company and our 43rd consecutive dividend since inception. The dividend of $0.33 US dollars per share will be paid on 24 May 2022, based on a shareholder record date of 13 May 2022. First, a couple of highlights. Yesterday, our Board formally approved the spin of FTAI Infrastructure from FTAI, and we expect the spin to be completed in the next four to eight weeks. Secondly, as to Russia-Ukraine war and our assets lost in that conflict, we are writing off $195 million US dollars in Q1 for impairments, bad debt, and lost revenue. We expect to recapture all of that $195 million US dollars over the coming year. Now let's turn to the numbers.
The key metrics for us are adjusted EBITDA and FAD, or Funds Available for Distribution. Absent the impact to our assets in the Russia-Ukraine war, which we estimate to be approximately $77 million US dollars in Q1, adjusted EBITDA would have been approximately $122 million US dollars, down 2% compared to $124.8 million US dollars in Q4 2021, and up 158% compared to $47.2 million US dollars in Q1 2021. Including one-time charges, actual adjusted EBITDA was $51.6 million US dollars in Q1 2022, which is down 60% compared to Q4 2021 and down 9% compared to Q1 2021. FAD was $71.4 million US dollars in Q1 2022, down 41% compared to $120.1 million US dollars in Q4 2021, and up 396% compared to $14.4 million US dollars in Q1 2021.
During the Q1, the $71.4 million US dollars FAD number was comprised of $117.1 million US dollars from our aviation leasing portfolio, $7.1 million US dollars from our infrastructure businesses, and -$52.8 million US dollars from corporate and other. Turning now to aviation, let's start with the impact of Russia's war in Ukraine. We reported Q1 2022 aviation EBITDA of $48 million US dollars. Write-off of uncollectible debt or canceled leases with customers that ceased operations reduced EBITDA in the quarter by about $70 million US dollars. We estimate EBITDA without the war effect would have been approximately $120 million US dollars or an improvement from Q4 2021 of $104 million US dollars.
In addition, we are writing off 100% of the book value of $125 million US dollars of the 12 aircraft and 20 engines that remain today in Russia or Ukraine. For those aircraft and engines, we have filed insurance claims totaling $290 million US dollars, which we ultimately expect to recover most, if not all, of this amount. When we do recover, all proceeds will be booked as income when received. We also took back nine aircraft from Russian and Ukrainian operators and are under LOI to sell four of these aircraft to cargo operators at a gain of approximately $30 million US dollars, while the remaining five aircraft are all 737NGs, for which there is very strong demand for both the aircraft and the engines.
We expect all nine of those aircraft to be on lease or sold by the end of Q2. We'll be taking further advantage of the strong cargo market and expect to sell other 747 and 767 aircraft and engines for significant additional gains in Q2. Turning to our aerospace products, we posted Q1 2022 EBITDA of $16 million US dollars, comprised mostly of income from CFM56 module sales again this quarter. Looking ahead, given the very visible and robust recovery in air travel demand worldwide, we're seeing a significant ramp in activity and backlog for our aerospace products. We currently have a backlog of approximately 180 modules contracted or on order and over $100 million US dollars of used serviceable material, USM, sales on order through multiple programs with MROs, maintenance and repair organizations, and airlines.
We continue seeing growing market acceptance of our CFM56 product offerings with today over 20 active customers, including many of the world's largest airlines and independent maintenance shops, and are importantly seeing a very high level of repeat usage. We expect demand to accelerate as heavy volumes of CFM56 shop visits are being scheduled now for H2 of this year. Let me now turn the call over to Ken to discuss infrastructure.
Ken Nicholson
CEO, FTAI Infrastructure
Thank you very much, Joe. We're excited about the prospects for our infrastructure business, and through the next few slides, I'm gonna talk about our recent results at each of our assets and highlight several of the projects and plans we have for growth in the coming months and the remainder of the year. It's an incredibly dynamic time in the transportation and energy markets with high commodity prices, extreme focus on energy security, and the mounting forces pushing energy transition, and we are in a great position with each of our businesses ideally suited to act on these opportunities. Starting on page nine with Transtar. Transtar generated $34.1 million US dollars in revenue and $14.6 million US dollars in EBITDA for the quarter.
Revenue was up $1.1 million US dollars or 3.5% quarter-over-quarter as slightly lower carloads were more than offset by higher average pricing. More specifically on carloads, cold-rolled steel shipments out of US Steel rebounded in March, showing promise for continued improvements next quarter, while hot-rolled coil shipments have remained steady. Shipment cycle times that were delayed at customers for unloading in Q4 and much of Q1 are moving at a faster pace, permitting Transtar's railcar fleet to turn more efficiently. EBITDA for the quarter was impacted, I apologize, by $2 million US dollars of non-recurring items and a lag in fuel surcharge revenue, meaning we experienced higher fuel costs in Q1 for which we will be reimbursed in Q2 due to the mechanics of our fuel surcharge program with US Steel.
Most importantly, cash flow from operations for the quarter was $16.6 million US dollars, in excess of adjusted EBITDA, as cash realized from the optimization of Transtar's railcar fleet was $3 million US dollars for the quarter, more than offsetting capital expenditures of $1.1 million US dollars. We're very excited about the future for Transtar. We're accelerating our commercial focus on third-party business, adding to our commercial staff, and pursuing a number of revenue enhancement programs. In total, we estimate an opportunity for approximately $30 million US dollars of incremental EBITDA over the next 12 to 24 months through these programs with minimal incremental capital need. Transtar is also an ideal platform for accretive acquisitions, and we're experiencing a growing pipeline of acquisition opportunities that we believe, if successful in acquiring, would be highly accretive to the business.
Turning to Jefferson. Q1 EBITDA of $3.8 million US dollars was up 35% compared to $2.8 million US dollars in Q1 2021, and up 66% compared to $2.3 million US dollars in Q4 2021, driven largely by strong ship dock utilization for inbound crude oil movements as well as the commencement of yellow wax crude by rail from the Uinta Basin. With the recent disruptions in global trade flows, Jefferson's multimodal infrastructure provides customers valuable optionality to handle volumes via marine, pipeline, and rail. For Q1 2022, crude oil and refinery intermediate revenues have grown 15% versus Q4 and 50% year-over-year. Volumes through the terminal have more than tripled versus Q1 2021 and have increased 32% versus last quarter.
From a project perspective, Jefferson remains on schedule for the end of the year and on budget for the previously announced 10-year deal with ExxonMobil. That project will bring substantial committed throughput volume and revenue to the terminal via our cross-channel pipeline system and provide a springboard for increased volumes. With the dislocation in the energy markets and demand by our refineries for more secure sources of supply, we're seeing growing activity at Jefferson. One of the emerging markets for crude supplies in the Uinta Basin of Utah, where volumes of yellow wax crude have been rapidly growing to replace imported barrels. At Jefferson, we moved an average of three trains per month through the terminal in Q1.
In Q2, we expect to move eight trains per month, and we have capacity of handling up to 24 trains per month, and that is our goal as we enter H2. Jefferson is the only terminal in the Beaumont region capable of transloading large quantities of yellow wax crude, and the process involves a significant amount of handling, heating rail cars to unload the product, and blending with lighter crude, so it's a particularly high-margin business for us. Turning to Long Ridge. We're pleased to report that our new 485MW power plant is up and running on a continuing basis, and we expect to generate strong cash flows under our power sales agreements for years to come.
In addition, we're taking advantage of our own natural gas assets to produce gas in excess of our power plant's needs for sale into the merchant market where gas pricing, needless to say, continues to be extremely strong. As the Q1 financials demonstrate, we took an unscheduled maintenance outage during the quarter to repair and complete commissioning of one of our steam turbines. The outage lasted approximately six weeks and represented an approximate -$8 million US dollars adverse impact on EBITDA for the quarter due to lost revenues during the outage. All costs to make the repairs were covered under warranty. While far from ideal, the outage did result in two positives.
First, we performed maintenance that was originally scheduled to take place in April, letting us avoid taking that outage and setting the stage for an uprate in power production to 505MW at little to no cost. Second, we completed our hydrogen blending project. In March, we became the first utility-scale power plant in the United States to run on hydrogen, starting with a 5% blend. This is an important development as the National Infrastructure Bill, which was passed last year, includes $8 billion US dollars of funding for the development of hydrogen hubs, and we have applied as a recipient. As an early mover with multiple advantages, Long Ridge is well positioned to secure funding from this program.
With the power plant in good shape, we're now focused on driving incremental growth by securing new business from power-intensive industries that want to locate new facilities at Long Ridge. We're seeing a robust pipeline of prospects and expect to announce our first major counterparty in the coming months. Finally, Repauno. Building on a successful first year of operation in 2021, we're kicking off the 2022 season in very good shape. Our business today is somewhat seasonal, with activity picking up in the month of April and continuing into Q4, so expect Repauno to generate solid results in Q2 and Q3 in particular. The newly expanded LPG truck rack has seen high utilization, providing both propane and butane to local heating and blending markets during a period of significant market volatility.
Our newly commissioned cavern chiller allows for fully refrigerated butane exports, and we have executed on a base agreement with an international offtaker for multiple cargoes beginning this month. We expect to move over 175 million gal of LPG in 2022 versus 130 million gal in 2021, with upside to over 250 million gal with spot movements which are on the increase. We continue to advance our build-out plans for additional product storage, increased rail access with the construction of a double unit train loop, 600,000 bbl of new storage, and pipeline connectivity to major production areas. We're finalizing permitting and construction contracting for the new storage facility, which will more than double our throughput capacity and triple cash flow potential once complete.
We expect to fund the capacity entirely with low-cost tax-exempt debt, making the expansion highly accretive. With that, let me turn it back over to Joe.
Joe Adams
CEO, Fortress Transportation and Infrastructure
Thanks, Ken. It's hard to imagine a 2-year period that's been more difficult and volatile than the last 2 years. Between COVID and the war in Ukraine, our business models have been stress tested in ways that we would never have expected. The good news is, FTAI has come through this period in good shape, and in fact, very good shape. The aviation industry is once again in growth mode, and our aerospace products are more in demand now than we had ever thought. With the world's rediscovered desire for more energy independence, our infrastructure assets are more critical today and more valuable than they were just two months ago. Putting it all together, it's a perfect time to separate the companies.
To that end, we filed this morning our public Form 10, which means that we should have two separate trading companies in the next four to eight weeks. Heading FTAI Infrastructure will be Ken Nicholson, who you just heard from. Ken has been my partner for over 20 years, including the last 10 since we started FTAI, and I'm very excited to be working with him in this new role. To sum it up, after years of preparation, the separation of FTAI Aviation and FTAI Infrastructure is now at hand, and we're very excited by the prospects for both companies. Turning back to Alan now.
Alan Andreini
Managing Director, Fortress Investment Group
Thank you, Joe. Tanya, you may now open the call to Q&A.
Operator
Certainly. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one on your telephone. To withdraw your question, please press the pound key. Our first question comes from Justin Long of Stephens. Your line is open.
Justin Long
Managing Director of Equity Research in Transportation, Stephens
Thanks and good morning. I wanted to start with aviation. Last quarter, you talked about the run rate for EBITDA from aviation being around $550 million US dollars, and that included $50 to 100 million US dollars from aerospace services. At the midpoint, if you strip that out, you know, aviation leasing was expected to do about $475 million US dollars of EBITDA. If you set Russia and Ukraine aside and take that out of numbers, what does that pro forma number look like going forward?
Joe Adams
CEO, Fortress Transportation and Infrastructure
Yes. I'll give you the answer first, and then I'll sort of walk back through how I get there. The answer, I think, for the year would be $475 million US dollars of EBITDA for both leasing and aerospace products. I would use $375 million US dollars of EBITDA for leasing and $100 million US dollars now for aerospace products. We're more comfortable, I think, at the high end of that earlier range, given the widespread acceptance and the backlog that we see building. If you take the $475 million US dollars and then you look at the $375 million US dollars for the leasing, as I mentioned, we had about $35 million US dollars of leasing EBITDA in Q1, and the war in Ukraine cost us about $70 million US dollars.
Call that, you know, roughly $105 million US dollars if the war hadn't happened for the leasing business. If you use that as a base, the assets that came off lease that I mentioned, you know, that are either off lease or stuck in Russia or Ukraine, figure that's about $20 million US dollars impact to Q2. We added business from the Avianca deal of about $10 million US dollars. Net-net, that's probably $95 million US dollars for Q2 from leasing. On top of that, we're gonna have, as I mentioned, a $30 million US dollars gain from a sale of the four cargo planes that we were able to get back. Call Q2 roughly $125 million US dollars.
Then if you look the balance of that to get to $375 or 380 million US dollars is about $220 million US dollars for Q3 and Q4. That's kinda how I get to that number. Hopefully that's helpful 'cause I apologize for all the variances and changes, but you know, this our world was sort of interrupted, unfortunately, as many people have been. That's the math.
Justin Long
Managing Director of Equity Research in Transportation, Stephens
That's extremely helpful. I know there's a lot going on. On that last point about the $220 million US dollars in the H2, does that assume any gains?
Joe Adams
CEO, Fortress Transportation and Infrastructure
No.
Justin Long
Managing Director of Equity Research in Transportation, Stephens
Okay. I guess, secondly on Jefferson, any update on what you're expecting in terms of EBITDA over the remainder of the year and how things could ramp? It was helpful to get some color on the trains per month that you're expecting in H2. Curious if you could put a sensitivity around that in terms of what one train per month means to EBITDA.
Ken Nicholson
CEO, FTAI Infrastructure
Yeah. Hey, Justin, happy to do that. Maybe to answer your specific question, one train per month, one train of yellow wax crude can generate, it depends, but anywhere up to $100,000 US dollars of EBITDA. It's significant. This is one of the reasons we're so bullish and so excited about it. You know, unloading one train can be a very high margin business between the heating involved, the blending and what have you. So it could be very substantial for Jefferson, and we're excited about the trend we're seeing here in Q2. You know, big picture with Jefferson, obviously, we have a lot going on. We've got the big Exxon contract kicking off at the early part of next year.
Our ultimate goal is, you know, to get Jefferson to $80 to 100 million US dollars of EBITDA. The precise trajectory for which we get there is, you know, I can't provide that kind of precision quarter-over-quarter, but our goal is at the end of the year and as we kick off the new Exxon business in January of next year, to be pretty close to that number on a run rate basis.
Justin Long
Managing Director of Equity Research in Transportation, Stephens
Okay, that's helpful. I appreciate the time.
Joe Adams
CEO, Fortress Transportation and Infrastructure
Thanks.
Operator
Our next question comes from Chris Wetherbee of Citi. Your line's open.
Chris Wetherbee
Senior Research Analyst, Citi
Yeah. Hey, thanks. Good morning, guys. Maybe just on the leasing side. I think, Joe, you mentioned that you'd recover, I think you said all of the $195 million US dollars that you're writing down. I guess I just could you help us sort of, you know, bridge that gap? Are you talking specifically about the leasing business, and is that just sort of new business opportunities that are out there? Is it a combination of that and insurance recoveries? I just wanna make sure I understand how you're thinking about that.
Joe Adams
CEO, Fortress Transportation and Infrastructure
Yeah, the recovering of the $195 million US dollars is really primarily would be from insurance and recovery of bad debt, not from any additional, you know, activity around that. That, that's what we were referring to in that. I think.
